articles.title: ★ A Week With the New Privacy Controls in MacOS 27.3 Beta 2
articles.summary:
On Monday, when the second betas of the v27.3 OSes came out, I posted about Apple adding the new privacy controls they had promised a month prior, in the wake of Meta’s Muse app surprising some users with what information it had access to (e.g. incoming iMessages) after being granted Full Disk Access — which authorization some users just clicked right through. I also posted a link to Apple’s corresponding new support documents. My initial take on Monday: 
I’m installing it now, but from what I’ve seen so far, these
changes not only alleviate my concerns that Apple might
over-tighten the screws, I actually think they add clarity and
give users more, not less, control over their Macs.
After a week, I’m willing to call it: this overhaul of these settings and permissions is a win. I really like the way that, for apps asking for Full Disk Access, users can now grant access to a list of folders instead. That’s what I mean about these new settings giving users more control.
Are these new dialog boxes “scarier”? Yes, and the point is, they should be. You should be slightly jolted into attention when an app prompts for any of these permissions. The question is whether they are unnecessarily scary. I would say no, not at all. The descriptions are fair and accurate. Is it unnecessarily scary to show you thumbnails of your personal photos before permitting Full Disk Access that would grant an application unfettered access to your personal photos? No! It’s a bit of a jolt to see them, but that’s just reducing the abstraction. The words “full disk access” feel different than actually seeing a snapshot of what full disk access entails.
Might this discourage some Mac users from granting Full Disk Access to AI agent apps? Yes. And it should! Users who actually understand the stakes will not be dissuaded by these new permissions. Additionally, I think these new dialog boxes represent very good UI design. They look like a new modern take on MacOS “system chrome” design — not skinny iPhone-sized alerts.
My only gripe about the new stuff is the prominent menu bar indicator that now appears when one app is controlling another. You can’t turn it off (except via an undocumented hidden defaults setting), and it’s distracting on most Macs, and extra distracting on the new MacBook Pros with PROLED displays because on those Macs, it appears in the Dynamic Island! Chance Miller, on Threads (with screenshots):
Most of the changes in macOS 27.3 are reasonable, but this Live
Activity thing for system access has got to go. It’s way too
aggressive.
It takes over the Dynamic Island on the new MacBook Pro!
As I write this article on a new MacBook Pro review unit, I have 8 of these indicators in my Dynamic Island: Scroll Reverser, Keyboard Maestro Engine, HazeOver, SteerMouse Manager, Moom, Chest (a promising new utility for managing menu bar icons), System Events, and a new text snippet expansion utility I’m beta testing.
Every one of these apps is running all of the time for me. This indicator being on, all the time, for every one of them isn’t helping me notice unusual activity. If anything, if Apple doesn’t rethink this idea, it’s going to make me miss the indication if an app is taking advantage of access permissions in an unwanted or unexpected way.
Zac Hall, Miller’s colleague at 9to5Mac, published an article on Tuesday showing the command-line defaults incantation to disable this. That’s better than not being able to disable it at all, but I expect Apple to revisit this based on feedback. It seems like a well-intentioned feature that was designed by people who didn’t realize how many always-on utilities “control other apps”.
articles.comment: 详细解读了macOS新版隐私控制，为用户提供了更精细的权限管理。
articles.reason: 及时分析了Apple新系统的关键隐私更新，对Mac用户非常有价值，且符合Apple生态主题。

articles.title: Linear scan register allocation in Datalog
articles.summary:
Note: This was supposed to be published basically immediately after PLDI 2026
but I got hung up on posting it because I am not a Datalog native like Yannis
is and I like understanding everything I post. But I guess that’s what expert
co-authors are for, right? It’s a little rough but it’s been so long that the
editing is holding up the posting. Happy reading.
Last year I wrote my first register allocator: a small
linear scan implementation in Ruby on SSA. Immediately after publishing the
post, I had a call with Waleed Khan where he walked
me through implementing the liveness fixpoint algorithm in Datalog. We talked
about doing the whole register allocator in Datalog—how hard could it
be?—but it never materialized.
This year, though, I met Yannis Smaragdakis at
PLDI. I did my usual thing, which is to nerd snipe other people into doing
interesting projects: in this case, full linear scan in Datalog. Several short
hours and several beers later, we have an implementation that I only mostly
understand.
Overall this is an excellent demonstration of programming in Datalog. It shows
tasks that Datalog handles very elegantly, such as the basic block computation
and the liveness analysis, which are just a handful of lines.
At the same time, it shows how to do things that are complex to do in Datalog,
namely the linear scan algorithm. The algorithm is very sequential,
imperative-style. It has steps such as “remove an interval that expires”,
“update the stack of intervals to evict the one ending last”, etc. All of these
operations have to be simulated declaratively.
The final result contains perhaps the most advanced Datalog programming
pattern, a forall emulation: iterating declaratively over a pre-determined set
(in this case, to select the interval corresponding to the variable to spill).
Let’s get into program representation.
Encoding
As with Waleed, we started off with the Wimmer2010 CFG example from the last
two posts.
 OUT.svg

digraph G {
node [shape=plaintext]
B1 [label=
B1(0:R10, 1:R11) 
2:jump →B2($1, R11) 
>];
B1:s -> B2:params:n;
B2 [label=
B2(3:R12, 4:R13) 
5:cmp R13, $1 
6:blt →B4, →B3 
>];
B2:s -> B4:params:n;
B2:s -> B3:params:n;
B3 [label=
7:B3() 
9:R14 = 8:mul R12, R13 
11:R15 = 10:sub R13, $1 
12:jump →B2(R14, R15) 
>];
B3:s -> B2:params:n;
B4 [label=
13:B4() 
15:R16 = 14:add R10, R12 
16:ret R16 
>];
}
-->




    
The graph from Wimmer2010 has come back! Again! Remember, we’re using block
arguments instead of phis, so B1(R10, R11) defines R10 and R11 before the
first instruction in B1.
Additionally, we have numbered the instructions in the graph. For each
instruction that defines a value, we have also given it two separate numbers:
one number N at which it uses its inputs and one number N+1 at which it defines
its output.
We do this so that the logic can process one event at a time: the end of a
liveness interval happens before the need to possibly allocate a register
because a variable gets assigned. This is visible in labels 8 and 9 as well as
14 and 15.
We have similarly modified block parameters: we sequentialize assignment by
picking different instruction indices for each block parameter in a block. This
is visible in labels 0 and 1.
This time, however, we encoded the program in terms of instructions instead of
in terms of blocks: we modeled which instructions used which registers and
def-ed which registers.

.type Block <: number
.type Var <: symbol
.type Instruction <: number

// Input
.decl var_use(insn:Instruction, var:Var)
.decl var_def(insn:Instruction, var:Var)

.decl jump(insn:Instruction, next:Instruction)
.decl jumpi(insn:Instruction, next:Instruction, otherNext:Instruction)
.decl ret(insn:Instruction)

#define NUM_REGS 2

// Facts: maintain the property that defs use a unique instruction so that
// liveness intervals end before the def
var_def(0, "R10").
var_def(1, "R11").

var_use(2, "R11").

var_def(3, "R12").
var_def(4, "R13").

var_use(5, "R13").

var_use(8, "R12").
var_use(8, "R13").
var_def(9, "R14").

var_use(10, "R13").
var_def(11, "R15").

var_use(12, "R14").
var_use(12, "R15").

var_use(14, "R10").
var_use(14, "R12").
var_def(15, "R16").

var_use(16, "R16").

.decl min_instruction(insn:Instruction)
min_instruction(-1).

.decl max_instruction(insn:Instruction)
max_instruction(16).

jump(2, 3).
jumpi(6, 7, 13).
jump(12, 3).
ret(16).


We also model the control-flow in terms of instructions: we have jumps between
instructions from which we (in Datalog!) recover the basic block boundaries and
control-flow graph (omitted for brevity). This is why we have jump(2, 3)
(which means jump at instruction 2 targeting instruction 3), ret(16)
(ret at instruction 16), etc.
Now that we have our program represented in Datalog, we can begin to compute
what we need from it… like liveness information.
Liveness
Since we complicated our input data a bit (variables are no longer def-ed in
blocks but instead def-ed in their own instruction indices), we had to expand
out liveness from the last post. Now we do a lot more in Datalog:
compute block boundaries (omitted for brevity)
compute what instructions are in what block (omitted for brevity)
compute the control-flow graph structure (omitted for brevity)
compute live-in and live-out for each instruction (not block!)
and finally, compute liveness intervals
Still, liveness is the most straightforward part of the implementation. There
are 4 rules defining live_out and live_in in mutual recursion. These
correspond to the standard data-flow equations in textbook definitions of
liveness. (The transfer function is encoded as two rules for explicitness, to
capture that a variable is live-in if it is used by the instruction, or if it
was live-out and is not def-ed.)

live_out(insn, var) :-
  block_succ(prev, succ),
  block_head(succ, headinsn),
  live_in(headinsn, var),
  block_tail(prev, insn).

live_in(insn, var) :-
  var_use(insn, var).

live_in(insn, var) :-
  live_out(insn, var),
  !var_def(insn, var).

live_out(insn, var) :-
  live_in(next, var),
  next_in_block(insn, next).


This looks similar enough to the liveness implementation that Waleed and I did,
but (as mentioned) handles instructions, not just blocks.
This only gives us the per-instruction sets, so to get the intervals, we need
to extract the full extents of the interval for every variable: the earliest
place it was known live and the latest place it was known live. We can use a
max and min here because we compute this only after the mutually
recursive dataflow has settled.

// Liveness starts right after start, ends right before end
.decl liveness_interval(start:Instruction, end:Instruction, var:Var)

liveness_interval(start, end, var) :-
  live_out(_, var),
  start = min b : { live_out(b, var) },
  end = max b : { live_in(b, var) }.


Once we have intervals, we need to assign physical registers to the
variables1.
Register assignment
The difficult part of the computation is the linear scan register allocation
itself. We encode this using a predicate reg_assignment which simulates what
the algorithm does at every step, with a linear scan of instructions.

// after instruction, this is the register assignment. Var = "none" is a possibility
.decl reg_assignment(insn:Instruction, reg:Register, var:Var)


At every
instruction, the algorithm keeps the current contents of registers that we are
allocating. Registers that are not currently encoding a variable are instead
holding a pseudo-variable that corresponds to the register’s name. E.g., when
register 0 is empty, it contains variable none_0. This encoding lets us
phrase every decision as a comparison between variables. The actual choice of
variable to spill, for instance, always prefers a “none” variable over a real
one, and then between real variables it implements the usual linear scan
policy: the spilled variable is the one whose liveness interval ends last.
Comments in the code explain all the cases that the algorithm needs to handle.
The assignment of values to registers is propagated if there is no liveness
interval that ends and no new variable that is def-ed (i.e., assigned).
When a liveness interval expires, the register holding the variable (if any)
gets reset to a “none” variable.
The interesting case is when we encounter a new variable def. We then need to
decide which variable to spill, i.e., which register (if any) should best
hold the def-ed variable. The policy for deciding on a victim variable is
entirely self-contained and modular, captured by predicate
better_victim_var, which pre-calculates the result of all possible variable
comparisons.
However, the interesting part is the forall emulation encoded in the rules for
predicates best_victim_up_to_reg and all_reg_best_victim. (The latter is
trivial to inline, but it’s kept for making the concept explicit.) The forall
emulation iterates over all registers and keeps at every point in the iteration
the current best victim variable. When we reach the final variable, we have the
overall best victim.
Returning to the core algorithm, if the victim variable is the def-ed var
itself, then all registers get carried over—the def-ed var does not receive a
register.
If, however, the best victim is a variable that is currently held in a register
then that register now gets assigned to the def-ed var, with all other
registers copied over to the next instruction.
Forall emulation is an advanced Datalog coding pattern. It arises in all cases
when a forall cannot be simply emulated as a “not exists”, because the
predicates involved are defined in mutual recursion. From a complexity theory
standpoint, the forall emulation pattern is essential for Datalog to be able to
encode all PTIME algorithms. (Although realistic Datalog implementations
include arithmetic and tuples, and hence are Turing-complete.) Without a
forall-emulation, which is possible only via an underlying ordering of values,
Datalog without extra features only expresses a subset of polynomial-time
algorithms.
The final step of the algorithm just assigns a register to a variable if the
variable can be held by the register for its entire lifetime. This is the
simplest implementation of linear scan—one could also extend it to allow
registers to hold a variable for a part of its lifetime.
Accordingly, there are many improvements to the implementation that one can
perform, especially for efficiency. Currently iteration is done over all
instructions, whereas it could instead jump from “interesting” to “interesting”
instruction, i.e., defs and interval expirations, ignoring instructions that
only copy over the register assignment. Additionally, the comparison between
two variables to find the best victim can be done on demand, instead of
calculating the result for all possible variable pairs up front. This would
require a request-response programming pattern, where the current rules only
fire in response to a request, i.e., only for variable pairs that truly need to
be compared in the course of execution.
Conclusion
Datalog is fun. It’s not for everyone or everything. But I love nerd sniping
people at conferences. Thank you to Yannis for playing along and writing half
this article and being so patient for it to be published!
See the implementation.
 end2;
   (end1 = end2, start1 > start2)).

/////// Final output
.decl assignment(reg:Register, var:Var)
assignment(reg, var) :-
  reg_assignment(_, reg, var),
  !spilled_var(_, var).

.output assignment
-->

  
In other register allocator implementations and in the
literature, we normally speak of assigning physical registers to
intervals, not to variables. However, in this one-interval-per-variable
implementation of linear scan, they are the same thing: a variable has only
one location for its entire lifetime. ↩

articles.title: This Week in Package Management: 21 November 2026
articles.summary:
This week’s package management news, gathered from the package manager OPML feed collection, my posts and boosts on Mastodon, and anything people sent me. Version control and forge news is in the Wednesday This Week in Source Control roundup.
Security
Gemstash 2.9.0 fixes eight vulnerabilities. The most serious is unauthenticated remote code execution through unsafe loading of upstream data (GHSA-27cp-f4p8-8qwv), rated CVSS 10.0. Non-default upstreams must now be listed in :allowed_upstreams, and upstream responses are capped at 64 MiB and 300 seconds.
The RubyGems team also announced that 2.9.0 is the last feature release of Gemstash. Vulnerability reports and bug-fix contributions will still be accepted, and the post lists several hosted and self-hosted alternatives. Mysteriously absent from that list: git-pkgs/proxy. An oversight, I’m sure.
Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14 fix seven vulnerabilities in Regexp and String case conversion, several of which can lead to remote code execution when an application compiles an attacker-controlled pattern. Ruby 3.2 and earlier are end of life.
Calif published details of Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a heap memory corruption bug in the AVX-512 Base64 decoder intrinsic in OpenJDK HotSpot on x86-64. The write-up reports pre-authentication remote code execution against Artifactory and other Java servers, and lists -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics as a workaround until the OpenJDK and vendor patches are applied.
pnpm 12.22.0 and 11.28.13 fix a bug where pnpm install could skip the minimumReleaseAge and trustPolicy checks against a new registry after the default or a scoped registry changed. 12.22.0 also adds a globalPackagesConfig section to the global config.yaml and pnpm why --ranges.
Bun 1.4.5 is a security release that updates its bundled lsquic, c-ares, SQLite, llhttp and BoringSSL.
Releases
RubyGems and Bundler 4.1.0 add an override method to the Gemfile that rewrites the version constraints dependencies declare, transitive ones included. override "foo", required_ruby_version: :ignore_upper installs a gem whose required_ruby_version cap excludes the current Ruby. Cooldowns now work in the gem command too: gem install --cooldown 7 skips versions published in the last seven days, and gem and Bundler each read the other’s cooldown setting.
An opt-in credential store writes the gem push API key and Bundler’s per-host credentials to the OS keychain instead of plain text files. The release also adds content addressable gems, with a --content-addressable flag on gem build, and ML-DSA support for signed gems (summary of six changes).
conda 26.10.0 makes Rattler the default solver for fresh installations and for upgrades without an explicit solver setting. conda config --set solver libmamba switches back to libmamba. The classic solver now ships as the separate conda-pycosat-solver plugin, and its built-in modules are scheduled for removal in 27.9. conda itself now requires Python 3.11 or newer to run.
pip-tools 7.7.0 is the first release since the project moved to the PyPA organisation. The project was in Jazzband for nine years, which is shutting down. The release requires pip 26.2.2 or newer and drops Python 3.9. A new stable extra caps pip at the latest version tested in pip-tools CI. It also fixes a bug from 7.6.1 in how PyPI JSON API URLs were built, which made resolution slower.
Stephen Rosen covers the release and Sviatoslav Sydorenko describes the move. After the repository transfer, releases to the pypi deployment environment required approval from a Jazzband team until the environment was reconfigured to use a PyPA one.
sbt 2.1.0 removes Apache Ivy from its dependencies, including from publishing. The metabuild moves to Scala 3.9 LTS, so plugins published with sbt 2.1.0 work only on 2.1.x.
In Docker Engine 29.10.0, setting insecure-registries in daemon.json or passing --insecure-registry replaces the implicit loopback exemption, and only the listed registries count as insecure. Pulls and pushes to a local registry over HTTP or with an untrusted certificate then require an explicit entry such as localhost:5000. Packages are now published for AlmaLinux, Oracle Linux and Rocky Linux.
mise 2026.11.9 (now 2026.11.11) adds lock pools, which give a task lock several slots, so a fixed number of tasks can use a limited resource such as CPU cores at once. --deny-unix and --allow-unix on mise exec and mise run block connections to Unix sockets such as an SSH agent or the container runtime socket, on Linux 7.1 or later.
Homebrew 7.0.15 now verifies Sigstore bundles in Ruby, after 7.0.14 vendored the sigstore gem and added a manifest_sha256 field to bottle blocks. 7.0.15 also bundles Ruby 4.0.10 for the Regexp and String security fixes.
Nix 2.36.0 reworks nix-daemon so workers re-execute the daemon with --stdio rather than forking, which lets most changes to /etc/nix/nix.conf reach workers without a daemon restart. Releases now ship nix-installer binaries for multi-user installs on x86_64-linux, aarch64-linux and aarch64-darwin.
uv 0.13.9 adds preview support for PEP 832 .venv redirect files for project environments and rejects wheels that an index lists under a different package name.
ORAS 1.4.0 moves to oras-go v3 and caches authentication per repository rather than per registry host, so oras copy can use different credentials for the source and destination on the same registry.
Also out:
vlt 1.8.2
npm 11.21.3
Gradle 9.9.2
Gradle 8.14.8
Maven 3.10.2
Swift Package Manager 6.4.3
APT 3.3.8
pipx 1.18.19
setup-uv 10.4.0
Dependabot Core 0.405.0
NuGet Client 8.2.0.18
Articles
Stricter checks for uploaded distributions on PyPI (William Woodruff, PyPI blog) describes new upload-time rejections aimed at parser differentials: sdists packed as V7-format tar archives, and wheels whose ZIP archive comment could be read as ZIP control structures. Two more checks are under evaluation: rejecting GNU-format tar sdists and rejecting any ZIP archive comment.
Introducing staged publishing on NuGet.org (NuGet blog). An uploaded package is validated and repository-signed but withheld from search and restore, even for its owner, until a maintainer with 2FA promotes it on the website. The .NET 11 RC2 SDK adds dotnet package stage push for the upload side, and promotion is website-only for now.
Farid Zakaria has two more posts on turning Nix builds into Bazel targets. Build systems à la trace records a build in the Rewind deterministic VM, treats each execve as a unit of work, models the result in MLIR and lowers it to Bazel genrules. GNU hello built this way produces the same NAR hash as cache.nixos.org.
Genrules all the way down uses his genrulify tool to transpile 219 Nixpkgs packages into 2,386 Bazel genrules, with each store path as its own target, and finds that Bazel runs fewer actions than Nix because it builds only what a target requires.
Elsewhere
beer.drv.drv.drv (Farid Zakaria) uses Nix’s experimental dynamic derivations to build a chain of 51 derivations, only the first of which exists at evaluation time. Each one outputs the next and prints a verse of 99 Bottles of Beer. Every step adds another .drv to the derivation name, and 50 bottles is the most that fits in a store path. He also found that nix-store --query --deriver returns unknown-deriver when the producing derivation is content-addressed, and filed NixOS/nix#16823.
The maintainer of mpld3 opened an issue looking for a new maintainer, and an account replied offering to help. His follow-up links ten similar offers the same account posted to ten other repositories within a minute, three days earlier, and he has left a warning on each of them.
Collaborations Workshop 2027 runs from 20 to 22 April 2027 in Cambridge, with research software quality and sustainable maintenance and funding among its themes. Applications to join the judging panel and for the Emerging Voices financial support scheme close on 11 December.
From Maintenance to Market (Sovereign Tech Agency and iconomy) is a 47-page report on how public investment in open source maintenance reaches European SMEs, with case studies and a Germany/France survey.
GitHub made security advisory permissions generally available, so custom roles can grant access to a repository’s security advisories and private vulnerability reports without granting admin. Dependabot alert dismissal requests now expire after a year instead of a week.
git-pkgs
